doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Cincinnati bands, race and the road to college
title: Hotels, shops and clubs that excluded black patrons
summary: Some stores and hotels were fine, but clubs like The Barn and The Hanger hired black musicians and barred black patrons, and the Lookout House was all white.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Let me ask you this. What about public accommodations, hotels, places to buy clothes?

Hotels, places to buy clothes, certain department stores were okay. Certain exclusive places were off limits. Nightclubs, certain places where black musicians might be able to play were off limits to black patrons.
For example? Does anything come to your mind?

There was a place called The Barn. It was a nightclub in downtown Cincinnati. Another place called The Hanger. These were just nightclubs, not dance halls, but just neighborhood bars. Black musicians played there, in trio or quartet format. Black patrons could not go in these places. The black musicians played there. One of the better-known dance halls was a place called the Lookout House. That was in northern Kentucky, somewhere near Covington. Black bands couldn’t even play in this place. They only had white bands, white patrons.
